clue.text: Costs are high — one's introduced cuts

indicators.note: the letters for one's are brought into the other fodder before it is shuffled
high in the sense of gone off or intoxicated, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: one is I, plus 's for is

explanation.surface: A complaint that prices are steep now that someone has brought in cutbacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high' shuffles COSTSARE with IS (from 'one's', brought in by 'introduced') to give the answer. 'cuts' looks like spending cuts but means snubs.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut someone is to snub them deliberately, the same as shunning them socially.

clue.text: British mostly in error — invisible border causing fuss

indicators.note: most of the word only, its last letter dropped

parts.note: out means wrong, as in a calculation being out
a ha-ha is a sunken fence or ditch that bounds a park without spoiling the view

explanation.surface: A British blunder over an unseen boundary sparks a diplomatic row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims OUT to OU. A ha-ha is a feature of English country estates: a ditch with a wall on one side, invisible from the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A brouhaha is a noisy commotion or uproar over something, which is a fuss.

clue.text: Comes to life again in bra and panties!

definitions.meaning: read as ...: someone who ... reverses dying

explanation.surface: A saucy exclamation about lingerie bringing someone back to life.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a playful coinage: split the word as UN + DIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Undies is the informal word for underwear, of which a bra and panties are the example.

clue.text: The Speaker's top dog

indicators.note: what a speaker says is heard, so a word for top is to be heard aloud

parts.note: a peak is the top of a mountain

explanation.surface: The Commons Speaker's finest hound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Speaker' looks like the Speaker of the House of Commons, but just means someone saying the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A peke is a Pekingese, a small toy breed of dog.

clue.text: Programme in a lot of trouble, right?

parts.note: big as in a big amount

indicators.note: the letter for right is placed in the middle of the other pieces

parts.note: bother is trouble or nuisance

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether a show is in serious difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the letter for right inside the trouble word. Big Brother is the reality TV programme named after Orwell's all-seeing watcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Brother is a reality television series, so it is a TV programme.

clue.text: Had nukes prepared … or a less effective weapon

indicators.note: the letters are worked into a new arrangement as something prepared

explanation.surface: Nuclear arms were readied, or else something feebler was to be used.
explanation.walkthrough: The skean-dhu is the small knife a Highlander tucks into his sock with kilt dress, a far weaker weapon than nukes.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish dagger is a weapon, and next to nuclear arms it is far less effective.

clue.text: "I won't!" Redhead on strike turned round, as expected

parts.note: a refusal is no
the head, or first letter, of red

indicators.note: the word for strike is read backwards

parts.note: to lam is to strike or thrash

explanation.surface: A redhead refuses to join a strike and does a U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redhead' is the first letter of red, not a ginger person; 'turned round' applies only to the strike word.
explanation.definitionFit: Normal means usual or standard, which is what happens as expected.

clue.text: 'E's crazy — First Noel a protest song!

indicators.note: the letters go wild and are rearranged

parts.note: 'E is a cockney he, with 's for is as a link

explanation.surface: Someone has gone mad, treating a Christmas carol as a protest anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' shuffles E and FIRSTNOEL. The Eton Rifles is a 1979 song by The Jam that mocks the upper class; Eton is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jam's hit about class conflict with Eton schoolboys counts as a protest song.

clue.text: New finish for race — it's Green Park

indicators.note: new means these letters are made into a fresh arrangement
the end of the word race, its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A race gets a fresh finishing line in London's Green Park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' shuffles E (the finish of race), ITS and GREEN. Green Park in the clue is a London park, a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is a famous Tanzanian national park, a park in the safari sense.

clue.text: "Whip's nothing", said the Member for Rotherham

indicators.note: the word is spoken in a Yorkshire voice, since Rotherham is in South Yorkshire

parts.note: nowt is northern English dialect for nothing

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire MP mocks the party whip as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip' reads as a party whip in Parliament, but it is a Russian lash.
explanation.definitionFit: A knout is a scourge once used for flogging in Russia, a kind of whip.

clue.text: Rake in money — the opposite is what normally happens

indicators.note: one word set inside another
the containment works the other way round from the clue's order, money going into rake

parts.note: a roue is a rake, a debauched man
tin is slang for money

explanation.surface: Advice to rake in cash, with a warning that the usual reverse applies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rake in money' suggests the rake goes inside the money; 'the opposite' says the money goes inside the rake instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A routine is the usual pattern of events, the regular practice.

clue.text: One not very good picking up runs? Hardly

definitions.text: One not very good picking up runs? Hardly

indicators.note: taking on board, so a letter is gathered inside

parts.note: a bad man is a person who is not very good
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A sneer at someone poor at scoring runs, swiftly rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Bradman, the Australian, is the greatest batsman in cricket history, so 'not very good' at 'picking up runs' is the reverse of the truth: 'Hardly'.
explanation.definitionFit: The famed Australian cricketer averaged nearly 100 with the bat, so calling him poor at scoring is ironic.

clue.text: Was sarcastic about shows lacking sensitivity

indicators.note: turned about, the letters are read backwards
the letters are on display within the words

explanation.surface: Someone was being sarcastic about stage shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' reveals SSARC inside 'Was sarcastic', and 'about' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass means stupid and insensitive, lacking tact or delicacy.

clue.text: Fencing by side of grass a joke?

indicators.note: one edge of the word, here its closing letter

parts.note: wordplay such as a pun is a verbal joke

explanation.surface: A pun about fencing beside a lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fencing' looks like a garden fence by the grass, but it is the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Swordplay is the art of fighting with swords, which is what fencing is.

clue.text: Readily accepts newspaper work — on reflection it's an easy choice

indicators.note: the word for readily takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: soon in the sense of willingly, as in I'd as soon go
FT is the Financial Times
op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: the word it is read backwards, as in a mirror

explanation.surface: Someone readily accepts newspaper work and concludes it was the easy route.
explanation.walkthrough: SOON takes in FT, OP and TI ('it' turned by 'on reflection'). 'Readily' meaning soon, as in 'I would as soon stay', is an older sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft option is the easier course of action, a choice needing little effort.

clue.text: Made American define a key change

indicators.note: the letters are changed round into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to define a key change, as in music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'key change' looks musical, but 'change' is the anagram signal on DEFINEAKEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Yankeefied means Americanised, given a US character, a Yankee being an American.

clue.text: Went home only occasionally — no fun at this lousy address

indicators.note: lousy means bad, so the letters are in a mess
only some of the letters are taken, every other one

explanation.surface: Someone rarely went home, given how miserable their address was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only occasionally' takes ETOE from 'Went home', and 'lousy' shuffles that with NOFUNATTHIS. 'address' is a speech, not a home.
explanation.definitionFit: The US President's yearly speech to Congress is an address, a formal speech.

clue.text: Looks at the writer talking rubbish

indicators.note: the pronoun is to be spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: the writer of the clue refers to themself as I
balls is slang for nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone looks at the author, who is talking nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball someone is to stare or look hard at them.

clue.text: Like some drinks in one boozer kept cool endlessly

indicators.note: the word for in is held within the other pieces

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a sot is a drunkard

indicators.note: the end of the word is cut off

parts.note: ice means to cool or chill
on as in the lights are on, i.e. in operation

explanation.surface: Some drinks are kept chilled in a pub, the boozer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kept' holds the word for in among the other pieces, and 'endlessly' trims the cool word. 'boozer' is a British word for a pub, but here a drunkard.
explanation.definitionFit: Isotonic sports drinks have the same salt concentration as body fluids, so the word describes certain drinks.

clue.text: Berks here groomed Rocky for battle

parts.note: Berks is Berkshire, a county in South East England, abbreviated SE

indicators.note: rocky means shaky or unstable, so the letters are shaken up

explanation.surface: Idiots in this place groomed Rocky, perhaps a horse, for combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Berks' looks like British slang for fools, but it is Berkshire, a county in the South East. Sedgemoor in Somerset saw the 1685 battle ending Monmouth's rebellion.
explanation.definitionFit: The Battle of Sedgemoor was the last pitched battle on English soil, fought in 1685.

clue.text: Washington idiot is in our party

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration
belonging to us, of us

explanation.surface: A political fool in Washington belongs to our side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washington' says the definition is American slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Doofus is American slang for a stupid person, a fool.

clue.text: River horse is caught

indicators.note: caught by ear, i.e. heard, so a word for horse is heard aloud

parts.note: a roan is a horse with a mixed-colour coat

explanation.surface: A hippopotamus, the so-called river horse, is captured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River horse' reads as the hippo, but 'River' is the definition. The Rhone flows through Switzerland and France.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhone is a major European waterway reaching the Mediterranean, so a river.

clue.text: See 8
Bribe keeps old worker cheerful

indicators.note: the word for bribe holds a letter within it

parts.note: to buy someone is to bribe them
an ant is the classic worker in crosswords

explanation.surface: A bribe keeps an elderly employee happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyant means in good spirits and lively, like cheerful.

clue.text: Champion's dark side ignored

indicators.note: one side, left, abbreviated L, is left out

parts.note: black means dark

explanation.surface: A hero's dark side is overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: The side is L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: To champion a cause is to back it, to support it.

clue.text: Stopped being right-on then?

definitions.meaning: ceased or paused, as in carrying on where you stopped
the opposite of right-on is ..., swapping each half for its opposite

explanation.surface: Was it giving up political correctness?
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading swaps right for left and on for off.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave off means to stop doing something, so left off means ceased.

clue.text: Ex and others getting upset

indicators.note: in a down light upset means turned over, read upwards

parts.note: et al is Latin shorthand for and others

explanation.surface: A former partner and others get upset.
explanation.definitionFit: Late can mean former, as in the late chairman, which is what ex means.

clue.text: Caught by shy rustic

indicators.note: next to, so the pieces are set side by side

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
to shy is to throw, as is to hurl

explanation.surface: A timid country person is captured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shy' looks like timid but is a verb, to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A churl is a peasant or boor, a rustic from the countryside.

clue.text: At risk surfing? Time he stopped

indicators.note: the pieces plug a gap inside the word for surfing, like a stopper

parts.note: surfing the internet means being online

explanation.surface: Someone surfing the internet is warned it is time to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surfing' looks like the waves but means being on the internet; 'stopped' plugs the other pieces into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Having something on the line means risking it, so the phrase means in danger.
